subtitle: In a disagreement, some messages are explicit and others depend on context. Understand both, and use inquiry to change your response without giving up the actual concern.
scope: For staff across DHS. Public concepts from the Intercultural Conflict Style model support original adult learning examples and private reflection. This course does not administer an inventory, classify a person or community, assess an IDI orientation or replace actual conduct and agency procedures. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA. Participation in this learning is voluntary.
introTranscript: Direct and indirect approaches concern how a substantive disagreement is communicated. Follow two practice adult volunteers who disagree about how a contribution should be described. Their personally learned meanings widen their first interpretations and change the next exchange. Practice checking a possible meaning, keeping the concern accurate and recognizing the limits of a learning example.

intro.heading: Locate how the substantive concern is communicated
intro.body:
Esme and Hollis are practice adult volunteers preparing a small community theatre display. They disagree about the description of a repaired prop. Esme proposes that the caption name the person who made the final repair. Hollis responds by describing how several earlier volunteers kept the prop usable over the years. The example supplies an attribution issue, an explicit proposal and a contextual response. It does not supply a final agreed caption.

In Mitchell Hammer’s public Intercultural Conflict Style model, direct and indirect approaches concern communication about substantive disagreements. A direct approach places greater emphasis on explicit verbal statements of the issue. An indirect approach places greater emphasis on context, history and relational messages. These are different ways a concern may be communicated, rather than a scale from honest to dishonest or able to unable.

Esme has explicitly proposed a named repair credit. Hollis’s history may be relevant to the disagreement, but its intended implication has not yet been supplied. Esme should not declare that he is avoiding responsibility; Hollis should not declare that her explicit wording means she rejects earlier work. The substantive question remains how to describe the contribution accurately and respectfully.

Outward emotional intensity is another dimension in the model. A quiet statement can be explicit, and an animated story can communicate through context. The course uses descriptions to teach the distinction without assigning either volunteer a core style or a formal inventory result. Their nationality, appearance or role would not settle what a particular message means.

Privately identify what is explicit, what draws on context and what still needs inquiry. You can use the example without sharing a personal conflict. A clearer understanding of your own first interpretation is useful even before an actual caption or work outcome changes.

items.title: Keep the actual issue visible
items.body: The disagreement concerns attribution on the prop caption. Reducing it to an awkward conversation would lose the question the volunteers need to consider. Wider understanding can improve how they approach that question without deciding that the final repair or earlier contributions should disappear.

items.title: Distinguish explicit content from implication
items.body: Esme states a proposal in words, while Hollis supplies a history whose intended implication is initially open. That is enough to examine message approaches. It is not enough to decide that he agrees, refuses or intends to deceive; those are additional interpretations needing support.

items.title: Separate approach and personal judgment
items.body: A direct statement can be considerate or inconsiderate, and a contextual message can carry a genuine concern. Neither category supplies conduct, motive or competence automatically. Learning to distinguish them lets a reader inquire rather than create a personal profile from one volunteer exchange.

tabs.label: Explicitness becomes the only sincerity
tabs.body: A reader treats only a plainly stated proposal as a genuine concern. Hollis’s history would then be dismissed before its meaning is heard. Explicit words are useful evidence, but the absence of identical wording does not establish that a contextual message has no substantive purpose.

tabs.label: Context becomes automatic agreement
tabs.body: A reader assumes the history is merely polite approval of Esme’s proposal. That interpretation skips the unresolved attribution concern. Listening for context should not become confident mind-reading; Hollis needs room to explain the meaning rather than have it assigned by the listener.

tabs.label: The issue and approach are separated
tabs.body: The reader retains the attribution question, identifies Esme’s explicit proposal and treats Hollis’s implication as open. This produces a useful inquiry without ranking the two people. A wider understanding may follow, while the actual caption decision and later experience remain unconfirmed.

check.question: Which account fits the opening example?
check.correct: Esme states a named-credit proposal explicitly; Hollis supplies relevant history whose intended implication remains open.
wrong: Hollis’s history proves he is dishonest.
Esme’s explicit proposal proves she rejects all earlier work.
Their message descriptions create official personal style profiles.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves the substantive attribution issue and the actual information supplied without inventing intention, agreement or assessment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A contextual history does not prove deception. An explicit proposal does not establish rejection of every earlier contribution. These learning descriptions teach a distinction; they neither administer an inventory nor establish personal profiles.

lessons.statement: Let the person’s meaning widen your interpretation without making it everyone’s rule.

intro.heading: Hear two learned meanings of respectful disagreement
intro.body:
Esme explains that she learned respectful disagreement while helping with letters for a local newspaper. A clearly named concern allowed another person to answer the point without guessing. For her, naming the final repair contributor expresses accountable recognition rather than an accusation that others did nothing. She initially experienced Hollis’s history as withholding the position needed for a fair reply.

Hollis explains that he learned respectful disagreement while preparing theatre rehearsals. Recalling earlier shared effort invited people to consider a relationship before changing how a contribution was described. For him, the history raises a concern that the caption could erase the continuing work of earlier volunteers. He initially experienced Esme’s isolated named-credit proposal as a dismissal of that shared effort.

These are personally supplied experiences, not rules for newspaper contributors or theatre volunteers. Esme can now understand the history as an attempt to keep shared contribution visible. Hollis can understand her explicit proposal as recognition that someone should be able to answer or correct. Their first judgments of evasion and dismissal are wider, while their attribution preferences may still differ.

The Council of Europe explains that cultural resources are used in personalized, internally varied and context-dependent ways. Hearing another meaning supports understanding of the other person and of the assumptions one brought to the encounter. It need not require a public autobiography, identical values or a work result.

Privately consider which first interpretation each volunteer can revise. You may reflect on a personally learned meaning of clarity or reciprocity without recording it, or remain with this example. Acknowledging another meaning does not require abandoning an accurate contribution or pretending the caption question is already resolved.

items.title: Understand named concerns as accountability
items.body: Esme’s explanation gives a reason for her explicit proposal: another person can answer or correct a clearly identified point. Hollis can recognize that purpose without deciding that only a single name belongs on the caption. The meaning changes his judgment of her intention, not every substantive preference.

items.title: Understand history as reciprocity
items.body: Hollis’s explanation connects the earlier work to a concern about erasure. Esme can hear the history as a contribution to the issue rather than empty evasion. She can still ask how that concern should affect the actual caption, keeping accountability and reciprocity in the conversation together.

items.title: Keep the learning personally meaningful
items.body: Recognizing a first assumption can enrich private understanding even if the volunteers have not chosen a caption. A learner need not produce evidence of workplace improvement to value that insight. The supplied practice histories allow meaningful reflection without compelling disclosure of family or community experiences.

tabs.label: His history must be evasion
tabs.body: This keeps Esme’s first interpretation after Hollis supplies a different meaning. It would dismiss the concern about prior work and make explicit wording a test of sincerity. She can instead recognize the relational purpose while asking about its substantive implication for the caption.

tabs.label: Her explicitness must be dismissal
tabs.body: This keeps Hollis’s first interpretation after Esme explains accountability. It would treat naming a contribution as rejecting all shared effort. He can recognize her reason and still explain what would be lost if earlier work disappeared from the description.

tabs.label: Meanings widen the interpretation
tabs.body: Each volunteer can understand why the other communicated that way and revise an initial intention judgment. The caption question remains. This allows genuine cultural self-understanding and a more considered exchange without ranking experiences, requiring identical preference or inventing a group communication script.

check.question: What changes after the two explanations?
check.correct: Each volunteer can revise a first intention judgment while retaining the unresolved attribution question.
wrong: Every newspaper contributor must prefer direct conflict.
The history requires Esme to abandon accurate repair credit.
Personal learning has no value until a work result proves it.
check.feedbackCorrect: The example supports wider interpretations through particular learned meanings, with both the underlying disagreement and intrinsic learning retained.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One personally supplied account cannot predict every member of a setting. Understanding reciprocity does not require erasing an accurate repair contribution. Private self-understanding can be meaningful before an actual decision or measurable work outcome.

lessons.statement: Offer an interpretation as a question and let the person correct it.

image.caption: Three people meet at a white table with laptops and notebooks; one uses a wheelchair.

intro.heading: Check an implication without putting words in someone’s mouth
intro.body:
Esme asks Hollis: Is your concern that naming only the final repair could leave the earlier volunteers’ work invisible? Hollis confirms that concern and adds that he is not asking for every previous volunteer’s name. The example now supplies a clearer substantive implication and a limit. It still supplies no agreed caption wording.

This question links the history to the actual issue while leaving room for correction. It does not announce that Esme knows his hidden motive or ask him to prove a cultural identity. A tentative interpretation can be useful when it states what the listener heard, identifies the possible concern and allows a different account. The person may also choose not to explain a personal history.

Hollis asks Esme whether her purpose is to make the repair claim answerable, rather than claim that one person created the entire prop. She confirms that distinction. Now both can separate a particular repair contribution from the broader history. Clarification has changed what they understand, without establishing the names, exact dates or other records that would be needed for a real display.

Directness and indirectness do not create a universal rule that everyone must confront someone face to face, use a third party or tell a story. The public model explains approaches; real choice, relevant conduct and actual formal procedures remain. The volunteer fiction permits a willing exchange, not a mandatory method for every disagreement or complaint.

Privately compare a tentative question with a confident motive claim. Hearing a boundary such as not every earlier name is itself useful information. You can learn through the supplied exchange without contacting a colleague, retrieving personal records or recording your own experience.

lessons.keyStatement: Offer an interpretation as a question and let the person correct it.

items.title: Tie the question to the supplied history
items.body: Esme’s question mentions the concrete attribution issue rather than asking Hollis to explain a whole community. It gives him a possible connection he can accept or correct. This keeps the concern understandable while avoiding a demand for identity details unrelated to the display.

items.title: Retain the clarification’s limit
items.body: Hollis wants earlier work visible but does not demand every name. Ignoring that limit would turn a clarified concern into a new exhaustive-credit requirement. A fair summary retains both what he confirmed and what he did not request; the exact caption remains undecided.

items.title: Do not force a preferred exchange
items.body: The example supplies willingness to answer. It cannot create a universal face-to-face or third-party requirement. A person’s boundary and actual formal procedures can matter, so learning to inquire should not become a reason to delay a complaint or compel a personal explanation.

tabs.label: Tell him his hidden intention
tabs.body: Esme declares that Hollis wants to deny the repairer credit. That goes beyond his confirmed concern and overlooks the explicit limit. A confident statement may sound efficient while misrepresenting the person; a tentative question gives correction room before action is based on the interpretation.

tabs.label: Demand every personal explanation
tabs.body: Esme requires a biography to accept that the history relates to attribution. The issue can be clarified without that disclosure. Relevant questions should serve the actual concern, and a person can decline a personal account without losing the ability to raise the substantive question.

tabs.label: Check the specific implication
tabs.body: Esme links the history to possible erasure and receives Hollis’s confirmation and limit. Hollis similarly checks her repair-credit purpose. They understand the disagreement more accurately while leaving the final wording and any actual factual verification open, rather than declaring universal agreement.

check.question: What has the clarification established?
check.correct: Hollis wants earlier work visible without every name, and Esme wants an answerable final-repair credit rather than a sole-creator claim.
wrong: Every earlier volunteer must be individually listed.
Esme has authority to invent missing repair facts.
A cultural biography is required before either concern is considered.
check.feedbackCorrect: This retains both confirmed implications and their limits; it does not invent wording, facts, disclosure or a completed choice.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Hollis explicitly does not require every earlier name. The practice discussion supplies no authority or evidence to invent repair facts. A relevant concern can be considered without demanding someone’s personal cultural biography.

items.text: Hollis wants earlier effort visible.
Esme wants the final repair contribution answerable.
Hollis does not request every earlier name.
Esme is not claiming one person created the entire prop.
The final caption is already approved.

intro.heading: Change the response while preserving the contribution question
intro.body:
Esme proposes beginning the next conversation by acknowledging the earlier work Hollis described, then considering a specific final-repair credit alongside it. Hollis proposes stating his concern about erasure more explicitly after that acknowledgment. Their response changes through the meanings they heard: reciprocity is received before the isolated credit is discussed, and accountability has a concrete concern to answer.

Neither change requires a compulsory praise formula or a story from every contributor. The point is that this response follows these particular meanings. Esme does not pretend the final repair never happened, and Hollis does not pretend the earlier volunteers never contributed. The offer preserves both questions instead of treating politeness as a substitute for accurate attribution.

The example does not supply final wording, verified repair records, agreement by an actual repairer or approval to publish. A real display would require its actual factual and permission responsibilities. In DHS work, clear communication likewise needs accurate conditions, roles and decisions rather than an attractive phrase that changes the information. Adaptation cannot authorize invented facts or conceal a remaining requirement.

A wider repertoire can include both explicit and contextual elements. Esme can receive shared history and still name a point; Hollis can state a concern without discarding the relational meaning. That flexibility is different from assigning one person a better style or declaring that everyone should always communicate indirectly.

Privately identify how the revised invitation reflects each meaning and one substantive question still open. You may value understanding the two purposes without producing a display. Optional work application remains possible where actual responsibilities, willingness and information support it.

lessons.keyStatement: Change how you approach the concern without hiding what still needs to be decided.

items.title: Acknowledge the meaning, not just the mood
items.body: Esme recognizes the role of earlier contribution in Hollis’s concern. This is more than saying the exchange was uncomfortable. Naming the actual purpose gives the next proposal a different context while leaving the final repair credit available for discussion rather than erasing it.

items.title: Keep accurate substance in the offer
items.body: A repair contribution and the earlier shared history are separate factual questions. Combining their consideration is useful, but it cannot supply missing facts or approvals. In a real publication, the responsible source and process still need to support what the wording says.

items.title: Leave the proposal genuinely open
items.body: Hollis offers a clearer concern after acknowledgment; neither volunteer claims the caption is already selected. Retaining that difference respects choice. The revised exchange can be meaningful learning while the actual decision remains unresolved, without using friendliness as proof of consent.

tabs.label: Erase the issue to appear considerate
tabs.body: Esme removes all repair credit so no one must discuss disagreement. That would abandon accountability without showing Hollis requested it. A considerate response can receive reciprocity and still examine the specific credit, rather than make silence the price of maintaining a relationship.

tabs.label: Require identical communication
tabs.body: The volunteers demand that both use only explicit statements or only historical stories. That would lose the wider repertoire their explanations made possible. A response can combine meaningful context with a clear concern, allowing different expression without confusing the actual issue or setting a universal style test.

tabs.label: Combine meaning and accuracy
tabs.body: They acknowledge earlier work and offer to consider a specific repair credit, with Hollis stating the erasure concern more plainly. The offer reflects both meanings and preserves substantive accuracy questions. It is a considered next exchange, not proof of publication authority, agreement or permanent resolution.

check.question: Which account best describes the changed response?
check.correct: They combine acknowledgment of earlier work with an answerable repair-credit concern while final wording and factual responsibilities remain.
wrong: Adaptation requires everyone to use one permanent style.
A welcoming offer proves consent to publish.
check.feedbackCorrect: This traces meaning to a concrete changed exchange and retains the distinction between a proposal, accurate substance and an actual decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Considerate language cannot authorize invented facts. A flexible repertoire does not require identical permanent styles. A welcoming offer is not evidence that affected contributors agreed or that the actual publication process is complete.

intro.heading: Separate communication flexibility from actual DHS duties
intro.body:
The theatre disagreement is a willing practice learning exchange. It supplies no agency complaint, personnel finding or publication authority. In real DHS work, understanding an explicit or contextual concern can improve communication while actual information, role and formal-analysis responsibilities remain. The course’s flexible conversation is not a substitute for those requirements.

Consider a separate supplied workplace example. Manager Dorian receives an allegation that a coworker has mocked an employee’s national origin. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment and discrimination to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Dorian cannot wait for a cultural explanation, a private reconciliation or completion of this optional course before that required report.

Dorian can communicate respectfully without deciding the allegation is true, false or resolved. The actual agency complaint and investigation procedures remain, including properly assigned investigation responsibilities and non-retaliation. The course does not appoint an investigator, prohibit authorized roles or give a manager permission to promise absolute confidentiality. A direct or indirect approach does not determine a legal outcome.

The program is led by the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant, who provides guidance, knowledge and feedback. Staff develop their own capacity to apply equity in their work. Resources may be used independently rather than every inquiry having to pass through the consultant. When an actual decision needs a specific responsible role or formal process, that responsibility comes from the work, not a new course-created gate.

Privately distinguish the volunteers’ optional meaning exchange from Dorian’s immediate duty. You do not need to handle a real complaint for learning to matter. In an actual situation, keep the concern and required response visible while communicating with care rather than making preferred style a reason for delay.

items.title: Keep the learning example in scope
items.body: The volunteers choose to examine attribution and meaning. It is not evidence about actual DHS conduct or a formal complaint outcome. Learning can widen a staff member’s repertoire without converting an original practice dialogue into agency procedure, delegated authority or a requirement to confront another person.

items.title: Report through the actual manager route
items.body: Dorian’s supplied protected-class allegation engages the immediate manager reporting duty. Cultural context may inform a respectful exchange, but it cannot be used as a gate to the report. HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and assigned agency procedures retain their actual responsibilities.

items.title: Build capacity without moving the work
items.body: Consultant leadership provides guidance and feedback as staff learn to apply equity independently. It does not mean the consultant performs every staff task or must approve every conversation. Actual role-specific decisions and formal analyses still need their real responsible process; independence does not invent authority.

tabs.label: Style explanation replaces reporting
tabs.body: Dorian asks everyone to agree on a culturally sensitive conversation before reporting the allegation. That would delay an immediate duty and could make participation a condition of access to the formal route. Understanding should support respectful communication while reporting occurs, rather than replace the actual process.

tabs.label: Independent learning becomes unlimited authority
tabs.body: A staff member assumes that using the course independently authorizes any publication or personnel decision. Resource access does not change delegated roles or actual evidence requirements. Staff ownership of work and appropriate consultant support can coexist with role-specific decisions and formal agency responsibilities.

tabs.label: Actual duty and thoughtful response coexist
tabs.body: Dorian immediately reports through the actual route and follows assigned procedures without making a finding. Staff can also seek guidance and communicate respectfully. This preserves both capability and responsibility, avoiding compulsory consultant approval and avoiding a style model as a legal decision tool.

check.feedbackIncorrect: Style agreement is not a prerequisite to immediate reporting. A voluntary course cannot decide or close an allegation. Program consultation is not a universal approval gate or a reason to delay the manager’s actual HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer route.

intro.heading: Recognize wider understanding without inventing resolution
intro.body:
The closing example describes these particular accounts. Esme now understands that Hollis’s history expressed a reciprocity concern, and Hollis now understands that her explicit proposal expressed accountable recognition. They offer the changed conversation described earlier. No agreed caption, verified publication facts or feedback from other contributors is supplied.

Those changes matter. The volunteers have a wider interpretation and a more considered way to approach the attribution question. Calling it a complete resolution would go beyond the evidence, but dismissing it because the caption remains open would lose meaningful understanding. The underlying disagreement and a useful learning outcome can coexist.

Hammer’s historical conceptual discussion distinguishes context and meaning from fixed personal traits and recognizes the capacity to adapt across situations. The Council of Europe likewise treats self-understanding and multiple perspectives as part of intercultural learning. These sources support a wider repertoire, not a course-based personal inventory or permanent label attached to Esme and Hollis.

In a real task, follow-through would require the actual concern, factual sources, choices and responsibilities. Staff might examine whether their summary reflects the person’s confirmed meaning and whether the next step is genuinely appropriate. The course does not require collecting personal stories or measuring an employee’s cultural development. A useful response does not guarantee every future exchange succeeds.

You may privately recognize a familiar first judgment: a contextual message as evasion, or an explicit point as rejection. Consider how another meaning could widen that judgment without losing an actual concern. Use the example if personal reflection is unwanted. This insight can remain unrecorded and worthwhile, while optional work application and actual agency duties continue in their appropriate places.

inThisLesson: Describe the particular changes and unanswered questions in the closing example.
Distinguish a wider interpretation from agreement, assessment or a completed outcome.
Explain how private self-understanding can remain meaningful alongside optional practical follow-through.
Which closing account is accurate?
lessons.keyStatement: Value the understanding gained and keep the unresolved question honest.

items.title: Describe the particular shift
items.body: Esme and Hollis each revise a first intention judgment through a supplied meaning. That is a supported change in understanding. Naming it precisely avoids both universal success claims and the opposite mistake of saying that no learning matters until all later choices are complete.

items.title: Keep the attribution question open
items.body: No agreed caption or publication facts are supplied at the close. The next real task would need its actual evidence and responsibility rather than a guessed ending. Retaining the open question makes follow-through more useful without labeling either volunteer a failure or deciding the display outcome.

items.title: Allow insight without a personal score
items.body: A learner can recognize an assumption privately and consider another meaning. That has intrinsic value, with no need to disclose a biography or classify a colleague. The practice route remains available, and formal inventories and actual conduct processes are not recreated by the closing reflection.

tabs.label: Understanding proves everything is resolved
tabs.body: This interpretation converts two particular meaning shifts into agreement about attribution and approval to publish. It removes the unknowns that still matter. A considered exchange can be progress without supplying a complete decision or guaranteeing the next contributor’s experience.

tabs.label: No practical result means no value
tabs.body: This interpretation ignores the volunteers’ wider understanding and would make private cultural learning depend on work proof. A changed first judgment can be meaningful on its own. Optional application can build from it without turning every reflection into an employee record or mandatory performance outcome.

tabs.label: Learning and uncertainty remain together
tabs.body: Recognize the wider meanings and changed offer, keep the caption and factual questions open, and preserve actual responsibilities. This is an accurate account of progress. It leaves room for private self-understanding and future practical inquiry without a score, forced agreement or an invented reassuring ending.

check.question: Which conclusion fits the full example?
check.correct: The volunteers understand each other’s meanings more widely and offer a changed exchange; final attribution and publication questions remain open.
wrong: Their course-based interaction produces official style profiles.
Their wider understanding proves every contributor agrees.
Private reflection is worthless without public proof of work improvement.
check.feedbackCorrect: This values the actual meaning shifts while preserving the substantive unknowns and intrinsic learning without assessment or guaranteed outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The course does not administer an inventory or issue a profile. Two volunteers’ understanding cannot establish every contributor’s agreement. Private self-understanding can matter without public work proof, and a practice reflection is a valid route to that learning.

items.text: Esme recognizes a reciprocity concern in the history.
Hollis recognizes accountable recognition in the explicit proposal.
The final caption wording is chosen.
Other contributors agree to the real publication.
The exchange creates official style profiles.
Private understanding counts only after a work score improves.

scenario.context: Consider this situation: A reader wants to call the attribution conflict fully resolved after the two volunteers understand each other’s meanings. No final caption is supplied.
options: Wider interpretation proves final agreement and publication approval.
No useful learning happened because the caption is not supplied.
Recognize the particular understanding and changed offer while retaining the open substantive questions.
responses: That invents decisions the example does not supply.
That discards meaningful understanding already supported.
This values learning without fabricating later outcomes.

lessons.transfer: Keep a changed interpretation private or use the example; no caption, personal score or public work receipt is required.

move.control: You can value a wider interpretation while accurately stating what remains open.
move.failure: A useful exchange becomes assessment, compulsory disclosure or guaranteed resolution.
move.next: Keep a changed interpretation private or use the example; no caption, personal score or public work receipt is required.

jobAid.title: Hear direct and indirect concerns more accurately
jobAid.subtitle: Connect message, personally supplied meaning and the actual issue without turning an exchange into a personal label.
jobAid.intro: Use the practice exchange or a private reflection; actual tasks retain their responsibilities.
remember: Directness concerns how the substantive disagreement is communicated, not a test of honesty or ability.
A personally supplied meaning can widen a first judgment without establishing a group rule or final agreement.
A learning exchange or consultant conversation does not replace actual agency roles, immediate reporting duties or formal procedures.

sections.heading: Read the issue and the message
items: Identify the actual substantive concern, explicit proposal and relevant context.
Treat an unclear implication as open rather than assume evasion, agreement or motive.
Keep emotional intensity separate from how explicitly the issue is communicated.

sections.heading: Check meaning and change the response
items: Offer a tentative interpretation connected to the issue and allow correction or a declined personal explanation.
Retain the confirmed meaning and its stated limits; do not add a requirement the person rejected.
Acknowledge relevant context while keeping accurate facts, genuine choices and the substantive concern visible.

sections.heading: Keep learning and duties clear
items: Value private self-understanding or a practice reflection without an assessment, biography submission or work-proof condition.
Managers and supervisors immediately report all protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow assigned agency procedures.
The consultant leads the program and provides guidance and feedback; staff retain work and may use resources independently, while actual responsible roles remain.

sections.heading: Describe the result honestly
items: Recognize a supported change in interpretation without treating it as final agreement or publication approval.
Keep missing facts and unresolved choices visible for appropriate follow-through.
Participation is voluntary; completion is not DHS-required training credit unless management, a director or DHS leadership expressly approves an exception.

sources.title: Mitchell Hammer: Solving problems and resolving conflict using the Intercultural Conflict Style model and inventory
sources.note: Selected original historical sections on direct and indirect approaches, context, meaning and adaptable responses. National and ethnic exemplars, inventory questions/scoring and historical usage statistics are not reproduced or used to predict people.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Explores varied meanings, multiple perspectives, self-understanding and action. Experiences in the examples do not determine personal assessments or group rules.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Actual immediate manager and supervisor reporting of all protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, assigned procedures and non-retaliation remain separate from the optional learning exchange.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual daily-work and relevant formal-analysis responsibilities remain; a conversation exercise neither completes a formal analysis nor creates new decision authority.

sources.title: DHS content and writing guidelines
sources.note: Clear purpose, accurate necessary information and actual roles support a real publication; an adapted response does not authorize invented facts or changed conditions.
